slides.heading: Junior AI Navigators, Week 8: Safe and Smart Online
slides.narration: [warmly] Welcome back to Ground School, Navigators. I'm Captain Naomi, and this is Week 8: Safe and Smart Online. Today we're learning how to check pictures, videos and voices, and what to do when something online doesn't feel right. Grab your grown-up and let's get started.

slides.heading: Pre-Flight
slides.narration: Our Pre-Flight plan fits in three little words: pause, check, ask for help. First we'll explore how pictures, videos and voices might be made or changed with AI. Then you'll practise asking three questions about surprising media. And your mission? Check some pictures, then make your very own Stop, Think, Tell poster.

slides.heading: Take-Off Question
slides.narration: Time for our Take-Off Question. Have a good look at this picture. There's a koala on a skateboard, right by the harbour. So, does this picture show an event that happened? Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Take-Off answer
slides.narration: This is an AI-generated picture. How do we know? Because it was made for this lesson, so we know exactly where it came from. And this is the big idea for today: looking believable does not prove an event happened. That koala looks convincing, and it still never skated anywhere.

slides.heading: Pictures, video and voices
slides.narration: AI can create or change digital media, like pictures, video and voices. With images, a scene might never have existed in front of a camera. With video, a clip might show something that did not happen. And with audio, a voice might be generated rather than spoken by that person.

slides.heading: What is a deepfake?
slides.narration: You might hear the word deepfake. A deepfake shows a real person in a false way. For example, AI can make a person appear to say words they never said. But not every AI picture is a deepfake of a person. Our koala isn't pretending to be anyone! So build this habit: check the source and the context before you believe something or share it.

slides.heading: Why was this made?
slides.narration: When you see a picture, it helps to ask: why was this made? The purpose matters. Some things are creative fun, like a clearly labelled made-up picture or story. Some are persuasion, a message trying to change what you choose. And some are deception, when someone tries to make you believe something that isn't true.

slides.heading: Ask three questions
slides.narration: So when something surprises you, ask three questions. One: is it plausible? In other words, could the event really happen? Two: who and why? Who made it or shared it, and what do they want? Three: how do I check? Find the original source, with a grown-up. Let's look at each one.

slides.heading: 1. Is the event plausible?
slides.narration: Question one. Is the event plausible? Notice when something gives you a reason to pause, like an animal doing a human activity, or something in an unusual setting. There's an important limit, though. Some real photos are so unusual they look unbelievable. So the next step is to check the evidence, rather than calling a picture fake just because of how it looks.

slides.heading: 2. Who made it, and why?
slides.narration: Question two. Who made it, and why? This is about finding the original source. Think about the creator: who made the picture or recording? Then the publisher: where was it first posted or published? And the purpose: is it labelled as made-up, is it an advert, a joke, or a factual report about something real?

slides.heading: 3. How do I check?
slides.narration: Question three. How do I check? This is one to investigate with a grown-up. First, read the context. Look for the original caption, the date and any explanation. Next, compare sources. See what reliable sources say about the same claim. And if the evidence is missing, just say, “not sure yet,” and don't share it as a fact.

slides.heading: Eyes and ears are not proof
slides.narration: Eyes and ears are not proof. Something can look convincing and still not be real. Sometimes odd details in a picture raise questions. But a picture with no obvious mistakes still isn't proven to be genuine. And hearing a voice you know doesn't prove that person really made the recording.

slides.heading: Instrument Check
slides.narration: Instrument Check! Does seeing or hearing something prove it happened? And your turn: what evidence would help you decide? Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Instrument Check: answer
slides.narration: Let's check your instruments. The answer is no, so check the source and the context. Pictures, video and sound can all be edited. Even a real image might have a caption that gets it wrong. So the best response is to pause, investigate, and ask for help.

slides.heading: AI is a tool
slides.narration: AI is a tool, and friendly words don't make it a person. A chatbot makes its replies using a computer system. So even when a reply sounds kind and personal, that doesn't mean it has human feelings, or that it cares about you the way a person does. When you have worries or something tricky is happening, the people you trust are the ones who help.

slides.heading: Big feelings? Tell a trusted person.
slides.narration: Big feelings? Tell a trusted person. You deserve help from a real human. Choose someone like a parent, a carer, a teacher or another safe adult. You can start simply. Try saying, “Something online worried me. Please help.” And if one person doesn't listen or help, keep asking. Tell someone else.

slides.heading: Stop. Think. Tell.
slides.narration: Here are three words to remember: Stop. Think. Tell. Stop means don't reply, don't click and don't send anything. Think means pause. You don't have to handle this on your own. And Tell means ask a trusted grown-up for help, straight away.

slides.heading: STOP
slides.narration: Let's look closer at Stop. Stop means pausing whatever is happening on the screen. If a message asks for something that worries you, don't answer it. If there's a link, don't click it or open anything more. Your next move is to step away from the screen and find a trusted adult.

slides.heading: THINK
slides.narration: Next is Think. This is where you notice pressure, or a feeling that something isn't comfortable. A warning sign is when someone wants you to act really quickly, or to keep a worrying secret. You don't need proof that something is wrong. Feeling unsure is enough reason to ask for help. Your job is to get help. The grown-ups handle the next steps.

slides.heading: TELL
slides.narration: And then, Tell. It helps to have a sentence you've practised. You could try, “I saw something online that made me uncomfortable.” Or, “Someone asked for private information. Please help.” And even if you clicked on something, tell anyway. [warmly] You still deserve help.

slides.heading: Privacy warning signs
slides.narration: Here are some privacy warning signs. If anyone online says things like, “Send me a photo of yourself,” or, “Tell me where you live,” or, “Keep this chat secret from your grown-up,” that's your signal to stop and tell a trusted adult. These are made-up examples, just for learning.

slides.heading: Private stays private
slides.narration: Private stays private, so keep your Never-Share List handy. Your identity: that's your full name, your address, your school and your phone number. Your accounts: that's passwords and login codes. And your images: don't send personal photos when someone online asks for them.

slides.heading: You deserve help, even after a mistake
slides.narration: You deserve help, even after a mistake, so tell without waiting. If you've already replied, you can still stop now and ask for help. If someone threatens you, don't try to make a deal with them, and don't send anything more. Tell a safe adult. And if you feel like nobody's listening, try another trusted adult until someone helps.

slides.heading: Mission: Real or Made-Up?
slides.narration: Mission time! It's called Real or Made-Up? There are three pictures and three questions. For each picture, talk with your grown-up about whether it could really happen, who made it, and what the evidence is. Then choose: is it a photograph, AI-generated, or not sure yet? After that, read the evidence reveal together.

slides.heading: Picture A: investigate
slides.narration: Picture A. This koala might look familiar! Time to investigate. Is it a photograph, AI-generated, or are you not sure yet? And what evidence would help you find out? Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Picture A: evidence
slides.narration: Picture A was AI-generated for this course. There's a record of it being made, and that record tells us where it came from. The scene shows something made-up. And notice this: we're not relying on odd details in the picture to prove it was generated. The record is our evidence.

slides.heading: Picture B: investigate
slides.narration: Picture B. Look carefully at this one. Is it a photograph, AI-generated, or not sure yet? What evidence would help you decide? Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Picture B: evidence
slides.narration: Picture B is a real photograph, and NASA has documented it. NASA says it's Apollo eleven image A S eleven, forty-four, sixty-five fifty-two. It shows Earth above the Moon's horizon. Our evidence is the space agency's original record, and that special image number.

slides.heading: Picture C: investigate
slides.narration: Picture C. A giant orange pyramid, sitting in a park. Is it a photograph, AI-generated, or not sure yet? And what evidence would help you decide? Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Picture C: evidence
slides.narration: Picture C was also AI-generated for this course. This imaginary jelly pyramid came from a tool that makes pictures. The record of how it was made backs up our answer. So our answer comes from evidence, rather than a guess based on how it looks.

slides.heading: What did the activity teach you?
slides.narration: So, what did the activity teach you? Evidence beats a confident guess. If you guessed correctly, explain what evidence backed up your answer. If you were unsure, that was a sensible answer before you saw the source. And if you guessed wrongly, use the new evidence to update your decision.

slides.heading: Make your Warning Lights poster
slides.narration: Now make your Warning Lights poster. It has three parts. Stop: don't reply, don't click, don't send. Think: pause and notice how you feel. Tell: ask a trusted grown-up for help. Pause the video and get creating with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Choose three trusted grown-ups
slides.narration: Next, choose three trusted grown-ups and make a private support plan. Do it together with your grown-up. Choose adults who listen to you and help you feel safe. Plan ahead: if the first person isn't around, how would you reach the others? And keep it private. Write their names in your own Flight Log, not in a public post.

slides.heading: Oops! Moment
slides.narration: Oops! Moment. Sometimes worrying about getting in trouble can stop us asking for help. The useful step is to tell a safe adult what happened. Here's a sentence to try: “I'm worried about telling you, but I need help.” And grown-ups, this bit is for you: respond calmly, thank them, and help with the problem.

slides.heading: Remember Rhyme
slides.narration: Here's a rhyme to remember. Stop, think, tell. A trusted grown-up helps as well! Say it together with your grown-up. Then practise: name the person you would go to first. Pause the video and have a go. [pause]

slides.heading: Quick Check 1
slides.narration: Quick Check one. What are the three steps if something feels wrong? Your turn: say the steps in order. Pause the video and say them out loud with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Quick Check 1: answer
slides.narration: How did you go? The answer is Stop, Think, Tell. Stop: don't reply, click or send. Think: pause and notice what's worrying you. Tell: find a trusted grown-up. [warmly] If you said all three in order, well done.

slides.heading: Quick Check 2
slides.narration: Quick Check two. Who helps with big feelings? Your turn: name a trusted person you could speak to. Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Quick Check 2: answer
slides.narration: The answer is a trusted person. That could be a safe parent, a carer, a teacher or another trusted adult. If you need more help, ask them to find the right support for children where you live. And keep asking. If the first adult doesn't help, tell another one.

slides.heading: Quick Check 3
slides.narration: Quick Check three. Name two things on your Never-Share List. Remember it from Week 2? Here's a hint: think about personal details, pictures and account information. Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Quick Check 3: answer
slides.narration: It's all about personal and account information. Any two of these are right: your full name, address, school, phone number, personal photos or passwords. And make sure you also protect your login codes and verification codes.

slides.heading: Your Flight Log
slides.narration: Time for your Flight Log. What will you do next time? Record it: draw your Stop, Think, Tell poster. Plan it: privately name three trusted grown-ups. And reflect: which source helped you check a picture today? Pause the video and fill in your Flight Log. [pause]

slides.heading: Grown-Up Corner
slides.narration: This one's for the grown-ups. Prepare support before there's a problem. If your child tells you about something, reassure them. Thank them for telling you, and avoid blame. Then act together, whether that's platform reporting, privacy settings or further support. And keep practising: revisit who to tell, and how to check surprising media.

slides.heading: Safe and Smart
slides.narration: Safe and Smart! You've earned your Week 8 Flight Log stamp. You practised checking the creator, the context and the evidence. You planned Stop, Think, Tell, and chose three trusted grown-ups. Next week is Build Week, when you'll plan and create your own project. [warmly] Great flying today, Navigators.
